The Septuagint is a Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures produced in Alexandria, Egypt around the third and second centuries before the common era for Greek-speaking Jews who no longer understood Hebrew. Begun during the reign of Ptolemy the Second, this translation became the Bible of Hellenistic Judaism and was the scriptural foundation of the early Christian church before most Christians read Greek.

Tradition holds that seventy, or possibly seventy-two, Jewish scholars were imprisoned on the island of Pharos and independently produced identical translations, hence the name Septuagint, which is Latin for seventy. The actual translation was likely gradual, piecemeal work over a century across different translators of varying skill, so the name is more mythic than historical. The translation was produced in Alexandria for Jews whose native language was Greek, not Hebrew, making the scriptures accessible to the diaspora who could no longer read the original. The Septuagint contains books not in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, including Wisdom, Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus, and the Books of Maccabees, which were included in later Christian Old Testaments in the Catholic and Orthodox canons but excluded by Rabbinic Judaism.

The Septuagint is earlier and sometimes more reliable than the Masoretic Text for reconstructing the original Hebrew scriptures, and modern critical scholarship often prefers Septuagint readings. The early Christian church used the Septuagint as its Old Testament and quoted it in the New Testament, especially in Paul's epistles and Hebrews. The translation was lost in the Christian Western tradition until recovered from ancient manuscripts in the seventeenth century. Scholars now edit it from Dead Sea Scroll fragments and medieval Greek manuscripts.
